Yesterday we learned that a judge has allowed a lawsuit seeking $32 billion to proceed, alleging that the facial recognition feature in Apple Photos violates state privacy laws.

Despite the two companies' drastically different approaches to privacy, this case has continually been conflated with Meta's use of facial recognition. In allowing the case to proceed, the court fundamentally misunderstands how this feature works...

Prior allegations against Meta

To properly understand the situation, we need to start with a facial recognition lawsuit against Meta that dates back to 2015.

Because that facial recognition was conducted on Meta's servers, and Meta was able to identify those faces, the company did indeed violate the law, and the case had merit, resulting in a $650 million settlement.

Apple is now being sued under that same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which prohibits companies from collecting biometric data without consent.

Apple's approach is fundamentally different

There is a major problem with this allegation: Apple absolutely does not collect biometric data to perform facial recognition within the Apple Photos app. As Apple noted in a 2021 machine learning research paper, the recognition algorithms run entirely on-device.

Furthermore, all the iPhone does is tell you "these photos look like they might be the same person" — it doesn't actually know who that person is. The only party capable of putting a name to those faces is the iPhone user themselves.

Apple Photos' privacy policy reflects this as well.

I am stunned that this lawsuit has been able to drag on through the justice system for six years when just a few minutes of research would reveal that the allegations in the lawsuit are plainly wrong.

Courts and legislators should be applauding Apple for this privacy-protective approach, rather than conflating it with the privacy-invading practices of companies like Meta.

This also further illustrates that the courts and legislators fundamentally do not understand the technology they are attempting to regulate. The most obvious example of this, of course, involves end-to-end encryption — multiple countries have threatened or attempted to ban end-to-end encryption without any understanding of how it actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in every area they need to address. But they have access to experts, and I am stunned that these lawsuits and draft bills can get so far without anyone pointing out these fundamental flaws.
